title: Curios of the Week #175
author: Ashman, Greg
summary: Greg Ashman's curios column #175 opens with an account of attending Edrolo's Melbourne hackathon, leaving him curious whether startup culture's iterative energy could be applied to schools. The substantive editorial content is a detailed critique of a new ASERA (Australasian Science Education Research Association) report on science education, which Ashman finds internally inconsistent: Alan Finkel's foreword articulates a sound position—that knowledge mastery remains essential even in an AI age, perhaps more so—but the report body surrounds this with progressive platitudes, relativist framing (calling knowledge 'knowledges'), and policy-committee recommendations so vague they commit to nothing. Ashman also speculates on Victoria's gender gap in calculus-based maths enrollment, proposing that boys' underachievement across all literacy domains may cause more of them to identify as 'maths people' through a relative-achievement mechanism. The column ends on multi-school charter and free school organisations, cut off before full development.
points: Alan Finkel's foreword to the ASERA report articulates a sound premise—critical thinking requires deep factual and technical mastery, and AI intensifies rather than reduces that requirement—but the premise is contradicted by the report's own content.

The ASERA report exemplifies the education policy committee failure mode: relativist framing ('knowledges'), avoidance of naming any evidence-based pedagogy as preferred, and recommendations so vague they commit to nothing.

The report's claim that the 'binary' between explicit teaching and inquiry is 'unhelpful' is a rhetorical move that allows inquiry learning to persist without having to meet the evidentiary bar applied to explicit instruction.

Ashman's hypothesis on Victoria's gender gap in maths enrolment: boys' underachievement across all literacy domains may cause more of them to identify as 'maths people' through a relative achievement mechanism—comparing themselves to others and finding a domain where they hold their own.

Startup culture observed at Edrolo raises an under-examined question for schools: which features of high-iteration, collaborative work environments could productively transfer to educational institutions.
quotes: The reality is that you cannot be a critical thinker if you do not have facts and knowledge at your fingertips. No matter how powerful the supporting AI, researchers and industry experts of the future will need to be deeply competent in maths, technology and science so that they can frame the prompts, evaluate the answers and create their own novel solutions to problems.
The report is desperate to appear groovy, nodding solemnly to climate change, AI and the 21st century at every opportunity.

Oddly for a report about science education, it calls knowledge ‘knowledges’—a relativist dog-whistle suggesting that there are no objective facts—and references ‘indigenous knowledges’ at every opportunity, but in a vague enough way that we don’t really know what that means.
ASERA does not recognise any one pedagogy as pre-eminent, but argues that the question of effectiveness is necessarily an interaction between purposes, pedagogy and context.

Ensure that science teacher educators are supported to recognise, represent and advocate flexible evidence-based pedagogies that reflect a variety of student outcomes and to effectively develop the professional judgments of teachers in responding to students’ diverse and complex learning needs.
The authorless EducationHQ piece notes the ASERA report’s platitudinous and entirely predictable mention of differentiated instruction and that’s where I came in.
I guess it’s what you write when you don’t know what you think or, in this case, when a committee cannot commit.
If you’re a young man and you see the people around you are better than you at writing, but you can hold your own when it comes to maths, you might start to identify more as a maths person.
